A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same financial red-teaming research, despite the renamed framework and benchmark. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack experiments across nine LLMs, including baseline comparisons, ablations, defenses, efficiency measurements, and human-versus-LLM judging.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds controller experiments, additional baselines and defenses, judge-agreement measurements, and controller sensitivity results.

M1.justification: v2 extends RCA into CoRT by adding a learned Risk Concealment Controller, an LLM-based concealment scorer, and online training from successful attack trajectories. The RoBERTa controller predicts scores that guide follow-up generation, substantially changing the procedure beyond renaming.

E1.justification: FIN-Bench becomes FinRisk-Bench, retaining the reported 522-prompt composition, six financial risk categories, category counts, and 240 benchmark-derived, 240 synthetic, and 42 FAQ-derived prompts. The added experiments retain the financial jailbreak task; newly documented expert review does not establish expanded coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds ActorAttack and X-Teaming to the main and efficiency comparisons while retaining the seven earlier attack baselines. X-Teaming supplies a substantially stronger reported comparator. The defense comparison also adds Self-Reminder and Goal Prioritization and removes the separate CoT entry.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controller training and validation protocols, including warm-up and online update schedules. Its defense comparison uses GPT-4o throughout, replacing v1's mixed GPT-4o/o1 comparison. Judge evaluation additionally measures accuracy and success-class F1 against human labels rather than comparing aggregate ASRs alone.

E4.justification: The multi-turn/feedback ablation gains a controller condition, and Appendix E adds nine warm-up/update-frequency configurations with validation and attack outcomes. Defense tests expand to both CoRT variants and additional defenses, while judge reliability gains agreement analysis. The earlier category and risk-trajectory plots are retained rather than newly added analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix C newly specifies random seed 42 in the controller training setup. Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the revision does not establish an increase in experimental repetitions.

E6.justification: v2 adds controller, baseline, defense, agreement, and sensitivity results, including 95.00% average ASR for RCA+RCC. Retained RCA scores also change, such as o1 from 97.56% to 97.89%. However, v1's category and risk-trajectory plots retain their values while being attributed to RCA+RCC in v2, creating an unresolved attribution inconsistency.

T1.justification: v2 introduces the bounded turn-level Risk Concealment Score in [0,1], its scoring rubric, and scorer-produced supervision. The atomic-call O(NT) time and O(T) per-query space arguments remain essentially unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from an adaptive two-stage RCA attack to learned, controllable red teaming with RCA and RCC. The abstract now distinguishes their reported average ASRs, 93.19% and 95.00%, and foregrounds controllability. The financial vulnerability and benchmark contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking controller learning to attack effectiveness and interprets the new baselines and defenses. It replaces v1's cross-model CoT explanation with a fixed-target defense interpretation. Limitations expand to omitted financial risk types, source and English-language biases, and changing regulatory interpretations.

D1.justification: New appendices document dataset quality control, controller inputs and training hyperparameters, NVIDIA L4 hardware, and added baseline configurations. Human evaluation now specifies 200 traces, three finance-background annotators, blinding, and majority voting. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing that every newly described procedure changed.

R1.justification: Positioning shifts toward learned controllability among modern multi-turn attacks. Related work adds ActorAttack, X-Teaming, ASJA, RACE, MRJ-Agent, and additional defenses. Gehrmann et al.'s financial safety taxonomy supplies substantive new context and motivates explicit boundaries on benchmark coverage.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution list, methodology, and experimental discussion undergo extensive rewriting. v2 introduces numbered subsections and reorganizes the appendix into sections A-I, alongside revised limitations and a dedicated ethics section. These changes exceed terminology updates accompanying RCA and benchmark renaming.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn to include the controller, several comparison and ablation tables are expanded or restructured, and Table 9 adds controller sensitivity results. The source-distribution figure moves into the main text, while category statistics move into the appendix. Document typography and page layout are extensively reformatted.

improvement.justification: Stronger baselines, fixed-target defense comparisons, human-agreement measurements, and fuller implementation details address weaknesses in v1. However, unchanged RCA plots are attributed to RCA+RCC, and v2 reports conflicting default-controller ASRs: 98.66% in Tables 1 and 5 versus 97.70% in Table 6. These unresolved inconsistencies weaken evidence for the central extension, limiting the overall quality gain.
